podcast.title: Arrest and Acquittal (April 21, 2001 - April 5, 2002)
podcast.body: Peter Buck was arrested upon landing at Heathrow following his air rage incident. His first trial collapsed, but at the second, three-week trial, he was acquitted on April 5, 2002. The jury accepted his doctor's testimony of "non-insane automatism," a condition where he "went nuts" instead of entering R.E.M. sleep, with Bono of U2 testifying as a character witness. "Peter was acquitted mainly because the jury bought the doctor's testimony of non-insane automatism."

podcast.title: Arrest and Charges (2001)
podcast.body: Following the in-flight incident, Peter Buck woke up in a police cell at Heathrow Airport, initially believing he was having a heart attack. He was subsequently charged with being drunk on a plane, two counts of common assault, and one count of damaging British Airways' property. "He thought he was having a heart attack and could understand why he was in this weird hospital Disneyland."

podcast.title: British Airways Air Rage Incident (April 21, 2001)
podcast.body: On April 21, 2001, R.E.M. guitarist Peter Buck boarded British Airways flight 48 to London, consuming a sleeping pill (M.B.N.) with up to 15 glasses of red wine. Instead of sleeping, he experienced "non-insane automatism," leading him to act wildly in the first-class cabin, ransacking it, flinging yogurt, and attacking crew members. "Peter pulled out a sleeping pill called M.B.N. and proceeded to wash it down with up to 15 glasses of red wine."

podcast.title: British Airways Flight 48 Incident (2001)
podcast.body: On April 21, 2001, prior to a scheduled concert for Nelson Mandela in London, Peter Buck boarded British Airways Flight 48. He combined a prescription sleeping pill, Ambien, with a large amount of red wine (reportedly 15 top-ups). This combination led to bizarre and disruptive behavior where he attempted to insert a CD into a food trolley, ripped up a formal warning card, grabbed a cutlery knife, smeared yogurt on himself and the cabin, and attacked flight crew members, almost causing the flight to be diverted for safety reasons. "Peter attempted to insert a CD into a food trolley, thinking it was actually a very big CD player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acquittal and "Non-Insane Automatism" Defense (2002)
podcast.body: Peter Buck's first trial collapsed, but at his second trial, which lasted three weeks and featured Bono of U2 as a character witness, he was acquitted on April 5, 2002. The jury believed doctor's testimony that the combination of Ambien and red wine resulted in "non-insane automatism," a legal term for non-voluntary behavior caused by an unusual drug-alcohol reaction, thus excusing his actions. "The combination of ambient and red wine resulted in something known as non-insane automatism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return Flight with British Airways (2002)
podcast.body: Despite the dramatic incident and subsequent legal proceedings, Peter Buck flew home to Seattle on British Airways after his acquittal. "And here's the best part. Peter flew home to Seattle on British Airways."

xref.title: Major Label Signing (1988)
xref.body: By 1987, R.E.M. felt they had exhausted their potential as an indie band and faced a choice between a career stall or signing with a major label. They signed with Warner Brothers on April 8, 1988, receiving a $6 million check. Michael Stipe stated the move was necessary for "worldwide" distribution, as IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit. Peter Buck reflected on the band's ongoing struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial moves, acknowledging they were "part of the machine." "So it came to pass on April 8, 1988, R.E.M. signed with Warner Brothers and took home a $6 million check."

xref.title: Peter Buck's Non-Insane Automatism Incident (2001)
xref.body: On April 21, 2001, R.E.M. guitarist Peter Buck, while flying British Airways Flight 48 to London, took a prescription sleeping pill (Ambien) and consumed 15 glasses of red wine, leading to a state of non-insane automatism. His actions included attempting to insert a CD into a food trolley, spilling its contents, ripping up a formal warning card, grabbing a cutlery knife, smearing yogurt, and attacking flight crew, nearly causing the flight to be diverted. He was arrested upon landing at Heathrow and charged with being drunk on a plane, common assault, and property damage. Buck was acquitted on April 5, 2002, after Bono testified as a character witness and a doctor explained the unusual drug-alcohol interaction. "The combination of ambient and red wine resulted in something known as non-insane automatism."

xref.title: Peter Buck British Airways Incident (2002) – "Non-Insane Automatism" Acquittal
xref.body: R.E.M. guitarist Peter Buck was acquitted in 2002 of violent behavior aboard a British Airways flight, which included attacking crew members and smearing yogurt on them. His defense successfully argued "non-insane automatism" — an unusual reaction between a sleeping pill (Ambien) and a large quantity of red wine that rendered him unaccountable for his actions. "Acquitted due to 'non-insane automatism,' caused by an unusual reaction between a sleeping pill and a large amount of red wine."

xref.body: The B-52s are mentioned as a group that began the Athens, Georgia music scene in the mid-1970s. Their success encouraged Peter Buck and Michael Stipe to form R.E.M. "The Athens, Georgia music scene, began in the mid 1970s with the B-52s and more obscure groups like the fans and pylon and the tone tones and love tractor and method actors."

xref.title: Balancing Art and Commerce
xref.body: Peter Buck articulated the band's struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial interests, expressing their fear of diluting the band's essence while acknowledging their role within the music industry "machine." Michael Stipe further explained the move to Warner Brothers by stating that IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit, necessitating a partnership with a label capable of global reach. "In our own case, R.E.M. is always trying to figure out where the line is between commerce and what we do, because it means something to us."

xref.title: Band's Love for Record Collecting
xref.body: The members of R.E.M. were avid record collectors, a passion notably influenced by guitarist Peter Buck, who used to work as a record store clerk. Michael Stipe was even one of Buck's regular customers. This love for records meant the band often took opportunities to go record shopping while on the road. "Now the guys in REM were all fans of collecting records after all guitarist Peter Buck used to be a record store clerk And one of his big customers was Michael Steip"

xref.title: Distinctive Rickenbacker Sound
xref.body: Peter Buck of R.E.M. is noted for his use of Rickenbacker guitars, the distinctive sound of which was crucial to the entire R.E.M. vibe from the very beginning of the band's career. The instrument's ancestry traces back to the first electric guitar in 1931. "The distinctive sound of these guitars was very important to the whole R.E.M. vibe from the very beginning."

xref.title: Formation Anecdote
xref.body: R.E.M.'s origins began when record store clerk Peter Buck initiated a conversation with art student Michael Stipe, who was often seeking out unusual 12-inch singles. Inspired by the success of friends like The B-52s, Peter and Michael later connected with Mike Mills and Bill Berry, two musicians from Macon, Georgia, to form the band. "a record store clerk named Peter Buck struck up a conversation with an art student who was always looking for strange 12-inch singles, and his name was Michael Steip."

xref.title: Formation and First Gig
xref.body: Guitarist Peter Buck, a record store clerk, struck up a conversation with art student Michael Stipe, who was often looking for strange 12-inch singles. Encouraged by the success of their friends, The B-52s, Peter and Michael recruited bassist Mike Mills and drummer Bill Berry, both from Macon, Georgia. Their first gig was at a friend's birthday party in a deconsecrated church in Athens on April 5th, 1980. "Shortly after the B-52s began to attract attention, a record store clerk named Peter Buck struck up a conversation with an art student who was always looking for strange 12-inch singles. His name was Michael Steip, encouraged by the success of their friends, the B-52s."
